title: Contributions from Cognitive Research to Mathematics and Science Education
venue: Proceedings of the Workshop on Research in Science and Mathematics Education
extended_summary:
This invited talk argues that cognitive science offers important guidance for improving mathematics and science education, but that the field’s evidence base is still limited. The paper frames a central problem in education as one of moving beyond mere information transmission toward helping learners construct usable knowledge, develop understanding, and eventually gain wisdom. It emphasizes constructivist assumptions: knowledge is actively built, prior knowledge shapes learning, learning requires purposeful effort, and understanding is often local and context-dependent.

The paper does not report a single intervention study. Instead, it synthesizes findings from cognitive research on misconceptions, novice–expert differences, chunking, categorization, and problem solving, largely drawing from physics and other science/mathematics domains. It also describes a curriculum-development model used by the author’s group, including the structure of expert knowledge and how novices differ in their use of conceptual and operational knowledge. These descriptions are used to propose pedagogical practices such as using multiple representations, helping students interconnect knowledge, extending context to refine concepts, and using comparisons and contrasts to build categories and relationships.

The context is higher-level science and mathematics education, especially introductory physics and related coursework, with examples drawn from classroom teaching and a large-enrollment introductory mechanics course. The main conclusion is that effective teaching should be interactive and communication-based, with instructors forming models of learners and designing activities that promote conceptual analysis, pattern recognition, and multiple-pass learning rather than one-pass information delivery. The paper also suggests that requiring qualitative analysis before solving problems can shift students toward more expert-like approaches.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an invited talk/proceedings piece presenting conceptual arguments and pedagogical recommendations rather than a controlled empirical study. It cites prior work but does not itself report a clear research design, sample, or tested intervention with outcome data.
impact_tier_rationale: No direct intervention effect is measured in this paper, so there is no estimable impact size on learner or institutional outcomes. The paper is influential as a theoretical framing piece, but evidence of impact is not reported here.
